semiconductor.title: Foreign talent programs, outside activities and conflicts
semiconductor.rule: CHIPS and Science Act s10632 (42 U.S.C. 19232) for federally funded research; company conflict-of-interest policy; Cal. Labor Code 96(k)/98.6 limits
semiconductor.requirement: Covered individuals on federally funded R&D may not participate in malign foreign talent recruitment programs and must certify compliance (verify applicability if the company holds federal research awards). More broadly, undisclosed talent-plan participation, side ventures and advisory roles are recurring facts in chip and AI theft cases. Employers can require disclosure of outside work, investments and affiliations related to their business, within state limits on regulating lawful off-duty conduct.
hrActions: Run an annual conflict-of-interest/outside-activity certification covering foreign talent programs, outside companies, advisory roles and investments
Require pre-approval for outside work in semiconductor or AI fields
Escalate red flags (founding a startup while employed, talent-plan applications) to Legal and Security
Apply the rules uniformly regardless of national origin
semiconductor.owner: Legal + HR + Security + Research Compliance (if federal awards)
semiconductor.risk: Undisclosed conflicts enable IP loss and, for federal awardees, can lead to award termination and false-statement liability.

source.title: Cornell LII - 42 U.S.C. 19232 (malign foreign talent recruitment program prohibition)

semiconductor.title: Taiwan national core key technology rules (brief)
semiconductor.rule: Taiwan National Security Act (2022 amendments on economic espionage involving national core key technologies); Cross-Strait Act travel-approval rules for covered personnel - verify articles
semiconductor.requirement: Taiwan criminalizes economic espionage involving government-designated national core key technologies (including advanced semiconductor process and related technologies) for the benefit of mainland China, Hong Kong, Macau or foreign hostile forces, with heavy prison terms and fines. Personnel on government-funded or commissioned core key technology projects need approval to travel to mainland China, including for a period after leaving (verify). Prosecutors used these provisions in 2025 in a case involving TSMC 2nm know-how (verify details). The Taiwan country file covers this in depth.
hrActions: Identify Taiwan roles that touch designated technologies or government projects and issue local-language notices
Align Taiwan onboarding and exit procedures with the Trade Secrets Act and National Security Act
Handle travel approvals for covered personnel
Forbid use of prior-employer (e.g., foundry) data by hires from TSMC and other fabs
semiconductor.cadence: Per hire, exit and travel request
semiconductor.risk: Criminal exposure for employees and damaged relationships with Taiwan foundry partners.

semiconductor.title: H-1B $100,000 fee, new fee proposal and wage rules
semiconductor.rule: Proclamation 10973 (Sept 19, 2025), extended Sept 18, 2026; DHS weighted-selection rule (effective Feb 27, 2026); DHS proposed 'Fee for Certain H-1B Petitions' (Aug 25, 2026); DOL prevailing-wage proposal (Mar 27, 2026); executive order on layoffs (Sept 18, 2026)
semiconductor.requirement: The $100,000 payment for new H-1B petitions for beneficiaries outside the US was upheld by the D.C. district court (Dec 2025) but vacated by the District of Massachusetts (June 8, 2026); the First Circuit denied a stay (July 24, 2026), and reports say it is not being collected (verify). On Sept 18, 2026 the President extended the proclamation to Sept 21, 2027 and ordered agencies to consider petitioners' recent or planned layoffs in H-1B decisions. DHS proposed a $103,265 fee on all cap-subject H-1B petitions, including change of status (comments about Sept 24, 2026); the FY2027 lottery was weighted by wage level; DOL proposed higher prevailing-wage levels (e.g., Level I moving from the 17th to the 34th percentile).
hrActions: Model H-1B cost scenarios for 2027 hiring (US-educated F-1/OPT graduates, cap petitions, hires from abroad)
Consider higher wage levels for strategic hires to improve lottery odds and prepare for DOL wage increases
Plan RIFs with Immigration: document selection criteria and H-1B/LCA effects before layoffs
Use Canada, India and Taiwan hubs and L-1/O-1 options as alternatives; update the mobility policy
Track litigation and rulemaking weekly before committing to fees in offers
semiconductor.owner: Immigration/Global Mobility + Talent Acquisition + Total Rewards + Legal
semiconductor.risk: Cost shocks and denials can derail hiring of foreign-born engineers, a large share of US chip design talent.

semiconductor.title: Security clearances and FOCI (if government work)
semiconductor.rule: NISPOM 32 CFR Part 117; SEAD 3 (reporting); DCSA FOCI process (SF-328)
semiconductor.requirement: Only if the company holds or seeks a facility clearance for classified work: appoint a Facility Security Officer and Insider Threat Program Senior Official, run an insider-threat program, report changed conditions (key management personnel changes, foreign ownership, control or influence), and make sure cleared employees report foreign travel, contacts and adverse information. FOCI must be mitigated, and foreign nationals cannot access classified information.
hrActions: Notify the FSO of key-management changes, cleared hires and terminations, and adverse information
Deliver annual insider-threat and security training for cleared staff
Coordinate debriefings at offboarding
Include FOCI review in equity-ownership and board changes
semiconductor.risk: Invalidation or revocation of the facility clearance and loss of government programs.

source.title: eCFR - 32 CFR Part 117 (NISPOM)

semiconductor.title: Lab, cleanroom and ESD safety for a fabless employer (brief)
semiconductor.rule: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1200 (HazCom, updated May 2024; compliance dates extended Jan 15, 2026) and 1910.1450 (labs); Cal/OSHA 8 CCR 3203 (IIPP) and 5194; Cal. Labor Code 6401.9 (workplace violence prevention); ANSI/ESD S20.20 (industry standard)
semiconductor.requirement: Fabless firms still run validation, characterization, reliability and failure-analysis labs (solvents and acids for decapsulation, compressed gases, lasers, X-ray, solder fumes, thermal chambers, high voltage) and send staff to foundry and OSAT cleanrooms. Employers need a written hazard communication program with SDSs, labels and training (OSHA pushed HazCom 2024 deadlines back four months, e.g., Jan 19 to May 19, 2026 - verify employer-specific dates), an IIPP and, in California, a workplace violence prevention plan. ESD programs protect product, not people, but need grounding and training. Reproductive hazards (e.g., certain glycol ethers, lead) call for informed, non-discriminatory handling of pregnancy: accommodations, no 'fetal protection' exclusions.
hrActions: Track EHS training by lab role in the LMS and block lab access until it is complete
Do job hazard assessments and provide PPE; brief travelers on site rules at foundry/OSAT sites in Taiwan and China
Give reproductive-hazard notices and run a pregnancy accommodation process (PWFA/FEHA) that offers reassignment without forced exclusion
Keep injury and illness records (OSHA 300; post 300A Feb 1-Apr 30) and investigate incidents
Update the HazCom program and retrain when SDSs and labels change
semiconductor.risk: OSHA/Cal-OSHA citations, injury claims and discrimination claims from mishandled reproductive-hazard policies.

globalFrameworks.title: RBA Code of Conduct v8.0: labor and ethics
globalFrameworks.rule: Responsible Business Alliance Code of Conduct v8.0 (effective Jan 1, 2024)
globalFrameworks.requirement: A customer-driven industry code. Labor: A1 freely chosen employment (no forced, bonded or trafficked labor; workers pay no recruitment fees and any fees found are repaid; no holding of ID documents; written terms in the worker's language before departure); A2 young workers (no child labor; under-18s kept from hazardous and night work); A3 working hours (at most 60 hours a week including overtime, except emergencies, and one day off in seven); A4 wages and benefits (legal minimums, overtime premiums, no disciplinary deductions, clear pay statements); A5 humane treatment; A6 non-discrimination and non-harassment (no pregnancy or medical tests used to discriminate); A7 freedom of association. It also covers Health & Safety, Environment, Ethics (business integrity, no improper advantage, whistleblower protection and non-retaliation, privacy, responsible minerals) and Management Systems, and applies to your own operations and your suppliers.
hrActions: Gap-assess own sites (US, Canada, India, Taiwan, China) against the Code, especially hours for lab and test operations and for contractors in Asia
Adopt an employer-pays policy for recruitment fees, including agency and dispatch workers in Taiwan, China and India, and audit labor agents
Make sure grievance and whistleblower channels meet Code expectations (anonymous option, non-retaliation)
Map policies to Code clauses for customer questionnaires
Train Asia HR teams on migrant-worker protections
globalFrameworks.owner: Supply Chain Sustainability + HR (Global Policy) + Operations + Legal
globalFrameworks.risk: Failing customer audits can cost design wins and supplier qualification with major OEM and hyperscaler customers.

source.title: Responsible Business Alliance - Code of Conduct

globalFrameworks.title: RBA VAP audits and customer flow-down
globalFrameworks.rule: RBA Validated Assessment Program (VAP), Self-Assessment Questionnaire, Corrective Action Plans; customer supplier codes and contracts
globalFrameworks.requirement: Customers often require suppliers (including fabless vendors and their foundry/OSAT partners) to complete RBA SAQs, pass VAP audits by independent RBA-approved firms (1-5 day onsite reviews with document review, worker and management interviews and site inspection), close priority findings through corrective action plans and closure audits, and cascade the Code to Tier-1 suppliers. RBA members commit to implementing the Code in their own operations and supply chains.
hrActions: Keep audit-ready evidence: time and overtime records, payroll, contracts, recruitment-fee records, age verification, grievance logs, training records
Prepare managers and workers for interviews without coaching
Own labor-section corrective actions with target dates
Work with foundry and OSAT partners' HR on migrant-worker findings
globalFrameworks.owner: Supply Chain Sustainability + HR Operations + Site leaders
globalFrameworks.cadence: As customers request; audit cycles vary (verify with each customer)
globalFrameworks.risk: Priority findings (fees, excessive hours, held IDs) trigger customer escalation and possible loss of business.

source.title: Responsible Business Alliance - Validated Assessment Program

globalFrameworks.title: UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights
globalFrameworks.requirement: Companies are expected to have a human-rights policy commitment approved at the most senior level, to carry out ongoing human-rights due diligence (identify, prevent, mitigate, track and communicate impacts on their own workers and supply chains) and to provide or take part in remediation, including operational-level grievance mechanisms. The UNGPs underpin the OECD Guidelines, the RBA Code and many customer and investor expectations.
hrActions: Publish or refresh a human rights policy covering forced labor, fees, hours, discrimination, freedom of association, privacy and health & safety
Include HR risks (contract labor, dispatch workers, interns) in the human rights risk assessment
Make grievance mechanisms available to contractors and supply-chain workers
Track remediation to closure
globalFrameworks.risk: Weak due diligence undermines defenses to forced-labor import detentions and customer audits.

source.title: OHCHR - Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights

globalFrameworks.title: OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises (2023 update)
globalFrameworks.rule: OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises on Responsible Business Conduct (updated June 8, 2023), Ch. IV Human Rights and Ch. V Employment and Industrial Relations; National Contact Points
globalFrameworks.requirement: Government-backed recommendations for companies operating in or from adhering countries (the US and Canada adhere): respect freedom of association and collective bargaining, give information to worker representatives, avoid discrimination, give reasonable notice and consult on major changes such as collective layoffs, and carry out risk-based due diligence across the value chain. The 2023 update added technology and data, climate and stronger protection for people who raise concerns. Complaints ('specific instances') can be filed with National Contact Points.
hrActions: Give reasonable notice and consultation in restructurings worldwide, beyond local minimums where feasible
Deal with worker representatives in good faith and without anti-union retaliation in every country
Map due diligence to the OECD six-step model
Monitor NCP cases in the sector
globalFrameworks.risk: NCP complaints lead to public findings; customers and investors reference the Guidelines.

source.title: OECD - Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises on Responsible Business Conduct (2023)

globalFrameworks.title: ILO fundamental principles and rights at work
globalFrameworks.rule: ILO Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work (1998, amended 2022); 10 fundamental conventions (C29, C87, C98, C100, C105, C111, C138, C155, C182, C187) plus the 2014 Forced Labour Protocol
globalFrameworks.requirement: Five fundamental principles: freedom of association and collective bargaining; elimination of forced labor; abolition of child labor; elimination of discrimination in employment; and a safe and healthy working environment (added in 2022 with C155 and C187). They bind states rather than companies, but appear in the RBA Code, customer contracts, investor policies and trade rules; the US has ratified only two fundamental conventions (C105, C182).
hrActions: Reference ILO standards in the global labor policy and supplier code
Treat occupational safety and health as a fundamental right in policies and metrics
Use the ILO forced-labor indicators in labor-agent due diligence
globalFrameworks.risk: Gaps show up in customer audits and investor questionnaires.

source.title: ILO - Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work

globalFrameworks.title: ISO 30414 human capital reporting
globalFrameworks.requirement: Voluntary guidelines for internal and external human capital reporting, covering areas such as compliance and ethics, costs, diversity, leadership, culture, health, safety and well-being, productivity, recruitment, mobility and turnover, skills, succession and workforce availability. Useful for consistent metric definitions behind 10-K Item 101(c) text and investor or customer questionnaires; certification is optional.
hrActions: Use ISO 30414 definitions for the internal human capital dashboard and metric dictionary
Choose a subset suitable for external reporting and document the formulas
Review what changed in the 2025 edition
Assess readiness for assurance
globalFrameworks.risk: Inconsistent definitions produce unreliable disclosures and audit findings.

source.title: ISO - ISO 30414:2018 (withdrawn; see ISO 30414:2025)

globalFrameworks.title: ISO 45001 occupational health and safety management
globalFrameworks.rule: ISO 45001:2018 plus Amd 1:2024 (climate action); revision (ISO/DIS 45001) under way
globalFrameworks.requirement: A management-system standard for occupational health and safety: hazard identification, worker participation and consultation, legal compliance, incident investigation and continual improvement. Customers and RBA audits often ask for it as evidence of health and safety management; certification is voluntary. The 2024 amendment requires considering climate change in the organization's context, and a full revision is expected.
hrActions: Align lab and office safety programs with ISO 45001 clauses
Set up worker consultation (safety committees) in each country
Report leading and lagging safety indicators to leadership
Plan for the revised standard's transition
globalFrameworks.cadence: Annual management review; surveillance audits if certified
globalFrameworks.risk: Without a recognized system, customer audits and incident defenses are weaker.

globalFrameworks.title: Forced-labor supply-chain rules (UFLPA; Canada S-211)
globalFrameworks.rule: Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (P.L. 117-78, effective June 21, 2022); Tariff Act s307 (19 U.S.C. 1307); Canada Fighting Against Forced Labour and Child Labour in Supply Chains Act (S.C. 2023, c. 9)
globalFrameworks.requirement: Goods made wholly or partly in Xinjiang or by UFLPA Entity List companies are presumed made with forced labor and barred from US import unless rebutted by clear and convincing evidence; electronics and semiconductor-containing goods are enforcement targets. Canada's Act requires entities meeting size tests (commonly two of: C$20M assets, C$40M revenue, 250 employees - verify) to file a report by May 31 each year on steps taken against forced and child labor; confirm whether the Canadian subsidiary is covered and whether 2025-26 amendments apply (verify).
hrActions: Run labor due diligence on labor agents, dispatch and contract workers, and student interns at OSAT/foundry partners in China and Taiwan
Check that no HR vendor or labor agent is on the UFLPA Entity List
Provide HR inputs (training, policies, grievance data) for the Canadian report
Offer worker-voice tools for the contractor workforce
globalFrameworks.owner: Supply Chain Compliance + Trade + HR + Legal (Canada)
globalFrameworks.risk: Shipment detentions, customer loss and penalties for false or missing Canadian reports.

source.title: DHS - Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act

globalFrameworks.title: Anti-corruption in hiring: relatives of officials ('princeling' cases)
globalFrameworks.rule: FCPA (15 U.S.C. 78dd-1; books and records and internal controls, 78m(b)); Foreign Extortion Prevention Act; EO 14209 (Feb 10, 2025); DOJ FCPA enforcement guidelines (June 9, 2025)
globalFrameworks.requirement: Offering jobs, internships or other benefits to relatives or referrals of foreign officials (including employees of state-owned customers, foundries, labs and universities) to win business is giving a thing of value. The SEC fined Qualcomm $7.5M (2016) over 'must place' hires of Chinese officials' relatives, and JPMorgan paid about $264M (2016) over its referral-hiring program. DOJ paused and then refocused FCPA enforcement (June 2025 guidelines prioritize cartels, harm to US competitors, national security and serious misconduct), but the statute and SEC accounting provisions still apply, conduct can be charged later within limitation periods, and local laws in China, India and Taiwan apply regardless.
hrActions: Ask in the ATS about relationships with government officials, SOE employees and customers; send flagged candidates to Compliance before offer
Route referrals from customers or officials through a documented, merit-based process
Keep internships open-application only; no customer-requested placements
Cover hiring risks in manager and sales anti-bribery training with annual certification
Keep hiring-decision records for at least five years
globalFrameworks.risk: Bribery and books-and-records liability, plus local anti-bribery exposure in China and India.

source.title: SEC press release 2016-36 - Qualcomm FCPA settlement (hiring relatives of officials)

globalFrameworks.title: Sanctions and restricted-party screening of people
globalFrameworks.rule: OFAC regulations (31 CFR Ch. V), SDN List and 50% rule; EAR Part 744; China Anti-Foreign Sanctions Law (2021)
globalFrameworks.requirement: US persons may not deal with SDNs or entities 50% or more owned by them, or provide services involving comprehensively sanctioned places (e.g., Cuba, Iran, North Korea and the Crimea/so-called DNR/LNR regions of Ukraine - verify current list). Hiring, paying or contracting with a sanctioned individual, or letting remote workers operate from sanctioned regions, can violate OFAC rules. China's counter-sanctions law can penalize compliance with foreign sanctions, creating conflicts for the China subsidiary.
hrActions: Screen contractors, freelancers, EOR workers and other payees (not only vendors) against consolidated lists at onboarding and periodically
Block remote work from sanctioned regions through policy and IP/geolocation controls
Screen expense reimbursements and travel involving sanctioned regions
Handle China counter-sanctions conflicts with Legal
Resolve name-match hits with documented review; never reject by nationality alone
globalFrameworks.owner: Trade Compliance + HR Operations + Payroll + Procurement
globalFrameworks.risk: Strict-liability civil penalties and reputational harm.

source.title: U.S. Treasury - Office of Foreign Assets Control

globalFrameworks.title: Global speak-up programs and government whistleblower awards
globalFrameworks.rule: DOJ Criminal Division Corporate Whistleblower Awards Pilot Program (Aug 2024, expanded May 2025); SEC whistleblower program (Rules 21F); FinCEN whistleblower proposal (Apr 1, 2026) covering BSA, IEEPA sanctions and related laws
globalFrameworks.requirement: Government award programs now cover corporate crimes including trade, tariff and customs fraud, sanctions violations, corporate immigration offenses and foreign corruption. A company that self-reports to DOJ within 120 days after receiving an internal report (and before DOJ contacts it) can still qualify for a declination, so fast, credible internal hotlines and investigations are needed in every country.
hrActions: Run a global hotline with local-language intake and triage within days; escalate possible export, sanctions and FCPA matters to Legal at once to protect the 120-day window
Enforce non-retaliation and monitor what happens to reporters
Follow local privacy and labor rules for investigations in China, India, Taiwan and Canada
Report metrics to the audit committee
globalFrameworks.risk: Slow internal handling forfeits self-disclosure credit, and retaliation creates separate liability.

calendar.title: Quarter-end blackout and mid-year equity review
calendar.detail: Quarterly blackout typically starts about two weeks before quarter-end (also Mar, Sep, Dec); mid-year review of burn rate, share reserve and peer group with the compensation consultant (typical timing).

calendar.title: Benefit plan filings and proxy-advisor surveys
calendar.detail: Form 5500 due July 31 for calendar-year plans (extension to Oct 15); ISS and Glass Lewis policy surveys typically run in summer.

calendar.title: Q2 10-Q and trading window
calendar.detail: Q2 10-Q with Item 408(a) disclosure; open window for pre-cleared trades and new 10b5-1 plan adoptions.

calendar.title: Policy and template review
calendar.detail: Annual review of insider trading, clawback, code of conduct and Rule 21F-17 carve-outs in employment templates; interim SOX testing of HR controls.

calendar.title: H-1B start dates, DSP audit and open enrollment
calendar.detail: Cap-subject H-1B employment can start Oct 1; annual Data Security Program audit and compliance certification (obligations since Oct 6, 2025); open enrollment; extended Form 5500 due Oct 15.

calendar.title: Q3 10-Q and next-year pay design
calendar.detail: Q3 10-Q with Item 408(a); ISS and Glass Lewis publish next-year policies (typical); compensation committee sets next-year plan design and metrics.

calendar.title: Year-end compliance close-out
calendar.detail: 409A deferral elections by Dec 31; year-end SOX controls for bonus accruals and equity true-ups; 280G and 162(m) modeling; annual export/TCP training and insider list refresh.

calendar.title: Export and sanctions re-screening
calendar.detail: Re-screen HR vendors, contractors and research partners against Entity List, SDN, UFLPA and DSP covered-person lists; review license-conditioned employees and TCP access.
